timeline: Baekje's early capitals, Wiryeseong and Hanseong, stood around today's Songpa District (the Pungnap and Mongchon earthen walls); Goguryeo took them in 475.
From 553 the lower Han River belonged to Silla, which set up Hansan Province, later called Hanju.
Goryeo made it Namgyeong (Hanyang), one of its three capitals.
In 1394 King Taejo of Joseon moved the capital to Hanyang, building Gyeongbokgung, the Jongmyo shrine and the city wall; it stayed the royal capital for five centuries.
Under Japanese rule from 1910 it was renamed Keijō (Gyeongseong), seat of the Government-General of Korea.
Named Seoul from 1946 and a special city from 1949; it hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics and is the capital of South Korea.
landmarks: Joseon's main palace, finished in 1395, burned in the Imjin War and rebuilt in the 19th century.
Both World Heritage sites: a palace laid out with its gardens, and the shrine to the Joseon kings.
It runs through the city, splitting Seoul into Gangbuk (north) and Gangnam (south).
specialties: Milky ox-bone soup simmered for hours, served with rice and kimchi — an old Seoul breakfast.
The Joseon palace kitchen tradition, built around five colours and five flavours.

dialect.name: Seoul speech
dialect.features: Standard Korean is based on the speech of middle-class Seoul; the intonation is flatter than in the south and sentences often end in -yo.

meme: Gangbuk vs Gangnam
Gangnam was only built up after the 1970s, yet it has become shorthand for 'expensive'; old Seoulites will remind you that every palace is in Gangbuk.

timeline: The area of the ancient Geochilsan state, later absorbed by Silla, centred on Dongnae.
Unified Silla made it Dongnae County.
Under Goryeo it was Dongnae Prefecture, already famous for its hot springs.
Joseon set up Dongnae-bu, with the Japan House (Waegwan) at Choryang for trade with Japan; the first battles of the 1592 Imjin War were fought at Busanjin and Dongnae Fortress.
Opened as a port in 1876, it became the starting point of the sea route to Japan; under Japanese rule from 1910.
Temporary capital during the Korean War (1950–1953); today South Korea's second city and biggest port.
landmarks: Korea's best-known beach, packed every summer.
Colourful houses stacked up a hillside, first settled by wartime refugees.
An old temple below Geumjeongsan, said to date from Silla.
specialties: Rice in pork-bone soup with chives and salted shrimp — everyday Busan food.
Cold wheat noodles that wartime refugees made from relief flour; found only in Busan.
Busan eomuk is known nationwide and sold in every market.

dialect.name: Gyeongsang dialect
dialect.features: It has pitch accent; speech is direct and clipped, and outsiders often think people are arguing.

meme: Baseball town
When the Lotte Giants lose, every taxi driver in the city will tell you about it; when they win, Sajik Stadium sings 'Busan Galmaegi'.

timeline: Known as Dalgubeol, part of Silla.
In 689 King Sinmun planned to move the capital to Dalgubeol, but never did.
Under Goryeo it was Daegu Prefecture.
From 1601 the Gyeongsang governor's office sat here; its herbal medicine market (Yangnyeongsi) has carried on ever since and was one of the largest in Joseon.
The 1907 National Debt Repayment Movement started here; under Japanese rule from 1910.
A directly governed city from 1981 (now a metropolitan city); Gunwi County moved in from North Gyeongsang in 2023.
landmarks: The old temple on the mountain north of the city.
Successor to one of Joseon's three great markets, busy at night.
A mural alley in memory of the singer.
specialties: Grilled pork intestines, Daegu's favourite drinking snack.
Thin, flat fried dumplings eaten with a spicy sauce.

dialect.name: Gyeongsang dialect
dialect.features: The same Gyeongsang family as Busan, with clear rises and falls in pitch.

meme: Daefrica
The basin is so hot in summer that people blend 'Daegu' and 'Africa' into 'Daefrica'; one street sculpture is an ice cream melting in the sun.

timeline: Said to be Michuhol, founded by Biryu; held by Baekje, then Goguryeo and Silla.
Under Unified Silla it was the Soseong area.
The Incheon Yi clan supplied several Goryeo queens and the town was raised to Gyeongwon-bu; from 1232 to 1270 Goryeo's court moved to Ganghwa Island to hold out against the Mongols.
In Joseon it held the port of Jemulpo; French and American fleets fought on Ganghwa in 1866 and 1871, and the Treaty of Ganghwa was signed there in 1876.
Jemulpo opened in 1883, with a Chinatown and foreign concessions; under Japanese rule from 1910.
UN forces landed here in 1950; Incheon International Airport opened in 2001; in July 2026 the city created the Jemulpo, Yeongjong, Geomdan and Seohae districts.
landmarks: Where Chinese merchants settled after the port opened, and one claimed birthplace of Korean jajangmyeon.
A World Heritage site together with the dolmens of Gochang and Hwasun.
A small island by the harbour, with rides and sea views.
specialties: Said to have been invented by Chinatown cooks for dock workers after the port opened.
Korean ginseng grown on Ganghwa Island.

dialect.name: Gyeonggi dialect
dialect.features: Close to Seoul speech; the northern islands such as Baengnyeongdo sound more like Hwanghae.

meme: The airport isn't in Seoul
Visitors say they 'landed in Seoul', but the plane came down in Incheon — locals have long since stopped correcting them.

timeline: The Baekje district of Usul.
Under Unified Silla it was Bipung County.
Under Goryeo it belonged to Gongju.
In Joseon it was just a big field under Gongju, called Hanbat ('great field') in Korean — the meaning of Daejeon.
It grew after Daejeon Station opened on the Seoul–Busan railway in 1905; the South Chungcheong provincial office moved here from Gongju in 1932.
A directly governed city from 1989 (now a metropolitan city); home to the Daedeok research district and the 1993 Expo.
landmarks: Korea's largest cluster of research institutes.
A spa town known since early times.
A red-clay barefoot trail on the edge of the city.
specialties: Open since 1956; people take the train just to buy its fried soboro bread.
Daejeon has one of the highest numbers of knife-cut noodle shops in the country.

dialect.name: Chungcheong dialect
dialect.features: Slow and drawn-out, often ending sentences in -yu.

meme: The boring city
Locals joke that Daejeon is a 'no-fun city' whose only sight is a bakery — and the joke has turned into a tourism slogan.

timeline: The southeastern coast of Silla.
Under Unified Silla it was Hagok County; the legend of Cheoyong is set at Gaeunpo.
Under Goryeo it was called Ulju.
Joseon's Gyeongsang Left Army Command was here; Ulsan's Japanese castle saw fierce fighting at the end of the Imjin War (1597–1598).
Under Japanese rule from 1910; Jangsaengpo was a whaling port.
Named a special industrial zone in 1962, where Hyundai's car, shipbuilding and petrochemical businesses grew; a metropolitan city since 1997.
landmarks: Whales and hunters carved into a rock face in prehistoric times.
Bamboo groves and gardens along the river.
One of the first places on the Korean mainland to see the sunrise.
specialties: Finely cut seasoned beef grilled on a wire grill.
Whaling is banned now; a museum and a whale village remain.

dialect.name: Gyeongsang dialect
dialect.features: The eastern Gyeongsang accent.

meme: Factory-town wages
Ulsan's income per head has long been among the highest in the country; buy a car here and someone will ask, 'A Hyundai?'

timeline: Part of Baekje.
Under Unified Silla it belonged to Ungcheon Province.
Under Goryeo it belonged to Gongju.
In Joseon it was the Yeongi area.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; Jochiwon grew up around the railway.
Created in 2012 and named after King Sejong, as an administrative city to which many ministries moved.
landmarks: Government buildings that run on for kilometres, with a garden on the roof.
The artificial lake at the heart of the new city.
Shaped like the pages of an open book.
specialties: The long-standing fruit of the Jochiwon area.

dialect.name: Chungcheong dialect
dialect.features: Long-time residents speak Chungcheong; newcomers come from all over the country.

meme: Friday in Sejong
It's a civil servants' city: on Friday evenings the express buses to Seoul fill up.

timeline: The Han River basin was Baekje's, then Goguryeo's in the 5th century, then Silla's after 553.
Under Unified Silla most of it was Hanju.
In 1018 Goryeo named the land around its capital Gaegyeong 'Gyeonggi' — the origin of the name.
Joseon's Gyeonggi Province surrounded the capital Hanyang; King Jeongjo built Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon (finished in 1796).
Under Japanese rule from 1910, still as Gyeonggi Province.
After 1945 its north was cut off by the dividing line; today it is South Korea's most populous province and, with Seoul and Incheon, makes up the capital area.
landmarks: King Jeongjo's walled city in Suwon, a World Heritage site.
Where King Injo took refuge in 1636, a World Heritage site.
A peace park on the Imjin River, close to the dividing line.
specialties: Icheon rice was once sent to the royal court; the town is also a pottery centre.

dialect.name: Gyeonggi dialect
dialect.features: Almost the same as Seoul speech, and one basis of the standard language.

meme: The commute
Two hours each way to a job in Seoul is normal; Gyeonggi people sleep on the subway better than anyone.

timeline: Land of the ancient Ye people, then Goguryeo, then Silla from the 6th century.
Under Unified Silla it was split between Sakju and Myeongju.
Under Goryeo it was Gyoju Circuit and the Eastern Frontier.
Joseon created Gangwon Province, named from the first characters of Gangneung and Wonju.
Under Japanese rule from 1910.
Cut by the 38th parallel in 1945; since the 1953 armistice there has been a Gangwon on each side. It hosted the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics and became a special self-governing province in 2023.
landmarks: The granite peaks of the east coast.
A lakeside pavilion for watching the moon and the sea.
specialties: Chicken and rice cakes stir-fried on a big iron pan.
Cold buckwheat noodles from around Chuncheon.
Highland potatoes are what everyone thinks of first.

dialect.name: Gangwon dialect
dialect.features: The east coast (Yeongdong) differs from the west; Yeongdong has pitch accent and often ends in -deuraeyo.

meme: Potato province
Mention Gangwon and people say 'potatoes'; Gangwon folk will hand you a potato pancake.

timeline: Fought over by all three kingdoms; a Goguryeo stele stands in Chungju.
Unified Silla placed two of its five secondary capitals here: Jungwongyeong (Chungju) and Seowongyeong (Cheongju).
In 1377 the Jikji was printed at Heungdeoksa in Cheongju — the oldest surviving book printed with metal type.
In Joseon it belonged to Chungcheong Province, named from Chungju and Cheongju.
Split off as North Chungcheong in 1896; under Japanese rule from 1910.
South Korea's only province without a coastline; Cheongju and Cheongwon merged in 2014.
landmarks: A World Heritage site together with other mountain monasteries.
A reservoir on the Namhan River.
Built on the site of Heungdeoksa.
specialties: Brined cabbage ready for making kimchi.

dialect.name: Chungcheong dialect
dialect.features: Soft and roundabout.

meme: No sea
To reach a beach you have to leave the province — so Chungju Lake is fondly called the 'inland sea'.

timeline: Both of later Baekje's capitals were here: Ungjin (Gongju, 475–538) and Sabi (Buyeo, 538–660).
Under Unified Silla it was Ungcheon Province.
Under Goryeo it belonged to Yanggwang Circuit and others.
In Joseon it was part of Chungcheong; Yi Sun-sin grew up in Asan, where the Hyeonchungsa shrine honours him.
Split off as South Chungcheong in 1896; during the 1919 March First Movement, Yu Gwan-sun led a protest at Byeongcheon in Cheonan.
The provincial office moved to Daejeon in 1932 and in 2013 to Naepo New Town between Hongseong and Yesan.
landmarks: Baekje sites in Gongju and Buyeo
Gongsanseong, Busosanseong and more — a World Heritage site.
Pine woods and beaches on the west coast.
specialties: Little walnut-shaped cakes, a fixture of motorway rest stops.

dialect.name: Chungcheong dialect
dialect.features: Slow, and never says 'no' outright.

meme: A Chungcheong 'no'
'Well, I suppose I could sell it for that…' translates as: that's far too cheap.

timeline: Old Mahan land, later Baekje; Iksan has the Mireuksa temple site and the Wanggung-ri palace site.
Unified Silla set up Wansan Province (Jeonju).
Under Goryeo it was part of Jeolla.
Jeonju was the ancestral seat of the Jeonju Yi, Joseon's royal clan, and Gyeonggijeon holds King Taejo's portrait; the 1894 Donghak Peasant Revolution broke out at Gobu (today's Jeongeup).
Gunsan port opened in 1899 and rice was shipped from it to Japan; under Japanese rule from 1910.
Split off as North Jeolla in 1896; renamed Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province in 2024.
landmarks: Baekje's largest temple site, a World Heritage site.
specialties: A brass bowl of vegetables mixed with chilli paste.
Bean-sprout soup with rice, Jeonju's hangover breakfast.

dialect.name: Jeolla dialect
dialect.features: Sentences often end in -ing or -dangkke; 'geosigi' stands in for almost anything.

meme: Nowhere bad to eat
In Jeonju you can walk into any restaurant and eat well — locals will only tell you the one next door is better.

timeline: A centre of Mahan, with large jar-coffin tombs along the Yeongsan River; later Baekje.
Unified Silla set up Mujin Province (Gwangju).
Goryeo's founder Wang Geon married into the Oh clan of Naju, which raised Naju's standing; 'Jeolla' comes from Jeonju and Naju.
In Joseon, Yi Sun-sin's Jeolla Left Navy was based at Yeosu; the 1597 Battle of Myeongnyang was fought between Haenam and Jindo.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; the Gwangju Student Movement broke out in 1929.
The Gwangju Uprising of May 1980; on 1 July 2026 Gwangju and South Jeolla merged into Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City.
landmarks: In memory of those killed in Gwangju in May 1980.
A path that appears from the sea a few times a year at low tide.
specialties: Salted, dried yellow croaker, once sent to the court.

dialect.name: Jeolla dialect
dialect.features: Close to the northern Jeolla speech, warm and expressive, often ending in -ing.

meme: Twenty side dishes
Order a set meal in Jeolla and the table fills with twenty-odd side dishes; visitors think there's been a mistake.

timeline: Home of Silla's capital Geumseong (today's Gyeongju); Daegaya's Goryeong is here too.
Gyeongju was Unified Silla's royal capital, where Bulguksa and Seokguram were built.
Part of Goryeo's Gyeongsang lands; Andong got its name ('east, at peace') after helping Wang Geon defeat Later Baekje.
In Joseon, Andong was a centre of Confucian learning, with Dosan Seowon and Hahoe Village.
Under Japanese rule from 1910.
Split off as North Gyeongsang in 1896; POSCO in Pohang and electronics in Gumi drove industry from the 1970s; the provincial office moved to Andong in 2016.
landmarks: Masterpieces of Unified Silla Buddhist art, a World Heritage site.
A yangban village of the Ryu clan, a World Heritage site.
A volcanic island in the East Sea.
specialties: Chicken braised in soy sauce with glass noodles.

dialect.name: Gyeongsang dialect
dialect.features: Andong keeps many old words.

meme: Yangban airs
Andong people are teased for their manners — even in an argument, seniority comes first.

timeline: The heart of the Gaya states, with Geumgwan Gaya centred on Gimhae; the Gaya tumuli are a World Heritage site.
Under Unified Silla it was Yangju and Gangju (Jinju).
Under Goryeo it was part of Gyeongsang.
In the Imjin War Jinju Fortress was besieged twice (1592, 1593); Yi Sun-sin won at Hansando, and the Three-Province Naval Command was later set up at Tongyeong.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; Masan and Jinhae were ports.
Split off as South Gyeongsang in 1896; Changwon, Masan and Jinhae merged in 2010 into Changwon, a machinery centre.
landmarks: Home of the Tripitaka Koreana, a World Heritage site.
Yi Sun-sin's naval base, the 'Naples of the East'.
Walls and the Chokseongnu pavilion above the Nam River.
specialties: Plain seaweed rolls eaten with side dishes, Tongyeong's speciality.

dialect.name: Gyeongsang dialect
dialect.features: The western Gyeongsang accent, a little different from Busan and Daegu.

meme: Jinhae cherry blossoms
Every April the Jinhae festival buries the city in blossom — and in traffic.

timeline: The independent kingdom of Tamna.
Tamna sent tribute to Baekje and Silla.
Goryeo absorbed it as Tamna County; the Sambyeolcho holdouts were crushed here in 1273, after which the Yuan ran horse ranches on the island.
Joseon made it Jeju-mok, often a place of exile — Kim Jeong-hui was banished to Daejeong.
Under Japanese rule from 1910.
Large numbers of islanders were killed in the Jeju 4·3 events from 1948; a special self-governing province since 2006, its volcanic island and lava tubes became World Natural Heritage in 2007.
landmarks: A crater rising from the sea.
specialties: A citrus with a knob on top.
Women divers who fish without breathing gear, recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage.

dialect.name: Jejueo
dialect.features: Very different from mainland Korean and keeps much Middle Korean; UNESCO lists it as critically endangered.
phrases: Thank you for your hard work

meme: Island of three plenties
Jeju calls itself rich in stones, wind and women; locals add a fourth: tourists.

timeline: The Han dynasty's Lelang commandery (108 BC–313 AD) is generally placed around Pyongyang; Goguryeo moved its capital here in 427, and its fall in 668 came with the loss of Pyongyang.
Unified Silla's northern edge ran roughly along the Taedong River, leaving Pyongyang a frontier.
Goryeo made Pyongyang its Western Capital, one of three; Myocheong's revolt broke out here in 1135.
In Joseon it was the seat of the Pyongan governor; the Taedong Gate and Ryongwang Pavilion were famous sights.
The American merchant ship General Sherman was burned on the Taedong in 1866; under Japanese rule from 1910.
Capital of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea since 1948.
landmarks: The east gate of the old city, rebuilt in Joseon times.
Hills by the Taedong River with the Ulmil and Pubyok pavilions.
Painted tombs around Pyongyang and Nampo, a World Heritage site.
specialties: Buckwheat noodles in a cool meat broth; many restaurants in the South carry the name too.
Mung-bean pancakes, a Pyongan home dish.

dialect.name: Pyongan dialect
dialect.features: North Korea's standard 'cultured language' is based on Pyongyang speech; sentences often end in -seumneda.

meme: The noodle debate
Pyongyang naengmyeon or Hamhung naengmyeon — which is the real thing? Food lovers on both sides can argue all night.

timeline: Land of the Okjeo and Mohe peoples.
Part of Balhae in the Unified Silla period.
Brought gradually under control from late Goryeo on.
In Joseon it was part of Gyeongheung, a frontier of the 'Six Garrisons'; Yi Sun-sin fought the Jurchens on Nokdundo in 1587.
Under Japanese rule from 1910, when Rajin port was built.
Made the Rajin–Sonbong free economic and trade zone in 1991 and a special city in 2010; it borders China and Russia.
landmarks: An ice-free port open to China and Russia.
The railway bridge between North Korea and Russia.
specialties: Fish and kelp from the northeast coast.

dialect.name: Hamgyong dialect (Six Garrisons)
dialect.features: The far-north frontier accent, often ending in -seumdung.

meme: Three-country corner
The only place in North Korea that borders Russia — from the Tumen you can see three countries at once.

timeline: Goguryeo heartland, home of the three Kangso tombs.
A frontier in the Unified Silla period.
Under Goryeo it lay around the Western Capital (Pyongyang).
In Joseon a small fishing village near Samhwa, called Jeungnampo.
Opened as the port of Chinnampo in 1897; under Japanese rule from 1910.
The West Sea Barrage was finished in 1986; today it is Pyongyang's port and a special city separate from South Pyongan.
landmarks: Goguryeo tombs painted with the Four Guardians, part of the World Heritage site.
A long dam and locks across the mouth of the Taedong.

dialect.name: Pyongan dialect
dialect.features: Close to Pyongyang speech.

meme: Pyongyang's sea gate
When Pyongyang people say they're 'going to the seaside', it usually means Nampo.

timeline: Ruled in turn by Baekje, Goguryeo and Silla.
Under Unified Silla it was Songak County.
Goryeo's capital Gaegyeong from 919 for nearly five centuries; Manwoldae is the palace site.
After Joseon moved the capital to Hanyang it became Kaesong-bu; its merchants (Songsang) were known for trading and their own bookkeeping.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; Kaesong ginseng was famous.
North of the dividing line after the 1953 armistice; the inter-Korean Kaesong Industrial Region ran here from 2004 to 2016; a special city since 2019, with Jangphung County added in 2023.
landmarks: Manwoldae, Sonjuk Bridge, the Songgyungwan academy and more — a World Heritage site.
Where Jeong Mong-ju was killed in 1392.

dialect.name: Kaesong speech
dialect.features: Historically part of the Gyeonggi dialect, close to Seoul speech.

meme: Kaesong merchants
'Kaesong people know their sums' is said all over the peninsula — double-entry bookkeeping is said to have early roots here.

timeline: The Goguryeo heartland; in 612 Eulji Mundeok crushed a Sui army at the Salsu (Chongchon) River.
A frontier between Balhae and Silla in the Unified Silla period.
Under Goryeo it was part of the Northern Frontier.
Joseon created Pyongan Province, named from Pyongyang and Anju.
Split off as South Pyongan in 1896; under Japanese rule from 1910.
Part of the North after 1945; the provincial office later moved to Pyongsong.
landmarks: On the Chongchon River at Anju, one of the 'Eight Views of Gwanseo'.
The battlefield of the Salsu victory.
specialties: Mung-bean pancakes, a Pyongan home dish.

dialect.name: Pyongan dialect
dialect.features: Flat intonation, with endings like -seumneda and -ni?

meme: The other Kansai
The 'Eight Views of Gwanseo' are in Pyongan Province and have nothing to do with Japan's Kansai.

timeline: Goguryeo land; its early capital Gungnae lay just across the Yalu.
Between Balhae and Silla in the Unified Silla period.
In 1388 Yi Seong-gye turned his army back at Wihwa Island on the Yalu and went on to found Joseon.
King Seonjo fled to Uiju in the 1592 Imjin War; Hong Gyeong-nae's rebellion began at Dabokdong, Kasan, in 1811.
Split off as North Pyongan in 1896; the Yalu railway bridge opened in 1911 and Sinuiju grew up around it; under Japanese rule from 1910.
Today the main gateway for trade with China, facing Dandong across the river.
landmarks: A famous mountain with the Pohyon temple.
A pavilion on the Uiju walls overlooking the Yalu.
The road and rail bridge between Sinuiju and Dandong.
specialties: A border crossing town with traffic across the river.

dialect.name: Pyongan dialect
dialect.features: The northwestern accent.

meme: The retreat from Wihwa Island
An army that said 'let's not, let's go home' — and ended up founding a five-hundred-year dynasty.

timeline: Early Goguryeo's heartland lay on both banks of the Yalu.
Part of Balhae in the Unified Silla period.
Brought gradually under control from late Goryeo on.
In Joseon it was the mountain country of Pyongan; King Sejong set up four counties here against the Jurchens.
Under Japanese rule from 1910.
Split from North Pyongan in 1949 as Chagang Province; mountainous, with large hydroelectric plants.
landmarks: Across it is Ji'an in China's Jilin, with Goguryeo's Gungnae fortress and the Gwanggaeto Stele.
One of the high ridges of the northern peninsula.

dialect.name: Pyongan dialect
dialect.features: A mountain accent that blends into Hamgyong speech at the edges.

meme: Across from an ancient capital
Stand on the Yalu and the Goguryeo capital of 1,600 years ago is on the other bank.

timeline: Goguryeo land; Anak Tomb No. 3 has rare ink inscriptions and murals.
Under Unified Silla it was the north of Hanju.
Close to Goryeo's capital Gaegyeong, a key area west of the capital region.
Joseon created Hwanghae Province, named from Hwangju and Haeju; the outlaw Im Kkeok-jeong roamed around Kuwolsan in the 16th century.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; the Yonbaek plain was a rice bowl.
Ongjin and Yonbaek south of the 38th parallel were briefly part of the South after 1945 and went to the North with the 1953 armistice; split off as South Hwanghae in 1954.
landmarks: A Goguryeo mural tomb, part of the World Heritage site.
Linked in legend with Dangun, and the hideout of the outlaw Im Kkeok-jeong.
Known in Joseon for calligraphy ink.

dialect.name: Hwanghae dialect
dialect.features: Between Gyeonggi and Pyongan speech.

meme: The outlaw's mountain
Im Kkeok-jeong's story has been filmed in both North and South, and it made Kuwolsan famous.

timeline: Goguryeo land.
A northern frontier in the Unified Silla period.
Close to Goryeo's capital; Wang Geon granted Pyongsan to his founding general Sin Sung-gyeom as the seat of the Pyongsan Sin clan.
In Joseon it belonged to Hwanghae Province — Hwangju gave half the name.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; the Seoul–Sinuiju railway ran through Sariwon.
Split off as North Hwanghae in 1954, with its office in Sariwon.
landmarks: A mountain fortress and the Songbul temple near Sariwon.
specialties: A well-known apple district of the northern peninsula.

dialect.name: Hwanghae dialect
dialect.features: A transition zone between northern and southern accents.

meme: Closer than you think
As the crow flies, Sariwon is far closer to Seoul than Busan is.

timeline: Land of the Eastern Ye, then Goguryeo; Silla pushed north to here in the 6th century.
The northern part of Sakju and Myeongju in Unified Silla.
Goryeo's Eastern Frontier.
In Joseon it was part of Gangwon (its north part in Hamgyong).
Wonsan opened as a port in 1880; under Japanese rule from 1910.
Divided by the 38th parallel in 1945; Wonsan and nearby areas moved from South Hamgyong into Kangwon in 1946; South Korean tourists could visit Kumgangsan from 1998 to 2008.
landmarks: White sands and sweetbriar roses near Wonsan.
specialties: The signature fish of the East Sea.

dialect.name: Gangwon and Hamgyong dialects
dialect.features: The south sounds like the Gangwon east coast; the north like Hamgyong.

meme: Two Gangwons
There's a Gangwon on each side, so elections and weather forecasts have to say which one.

timeline: Land of the Okjeo, then Goguryeo; in the 6th century Silla's King Jinheung set up the Hwangchoryong and Maunryong steles here.
Part of Balhae in the Unified Silla period.
Brought under control in late Goryeo; Yi Seong-gye's family rose to power here.
Joseon's Hamgyong Province (from Hamhung and Gyeongseong); King Taejo retired to Hamhung, giving rise to the phrase 'Hamhung envoy'.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; large chemical works were built at Hungnam.
The Battle of Chosin Reservoir and the Hungnam evacuation took place here in the winter of 1950.
specialties: Chewy noodles of potato starch, with spicy raw fish.

dialect.name: Hamgyong dialect
dialect.features: Pitch accent, with endings like -seumdung and -mme.

meme: The Hamhung envoy
None of the envoys sent to fetch the retired king from Hamhung ever came back — so a 'Hamhung envoy' is someone who goes and never returns.

timeline: Land of the Okjeo and Mohe.
Part of Balhae in the Unified Silla period.
Under Goryeo, Jurchen country.
Under King Sejong, Kim Jong-seo founded the 'Six Garrisons', pushing the border to the Tumen; Gyeongseong gave half the province's name.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; Chongjin grew into a port and industrial city.
Part of the North after 1945; the provincial office is in Chongjin.
landmarks: A coastal mountain of strange rocks.
A northern stronghold in Joseon times.

dialect.name: Hamgyong dialect (Six Garrisons)
dialect.features: Keeps many Middle Korean forms; sentences often end in -mdung.

meme: The Six Garrisons
King Sejong's 'northern frontier' made the Tumen River the peninsula's northern border.

timeline: The Paektu area, a frontier of Goguryeo and Balhae.
Part of Balhae in the Unified Silla period.
Under Goryeo, Jurchen country.
In Joseon it belonged to Hamgyong; a boundary stele was set up on Paektu in 1712.
Under Japanese rule from 1910; the Battle of Pochonbo took place in 1937.
Created in 1954 from parts of South and North Hamgyong as Ryanggang Province.
landmarks: A crater lake on the peninsula's highest peak; the China–North Korea border crosses it.

dialect.name: Hamgyong dialect
dialect.features: A northern accent.

meme: The coldest province
Minus thirty or forty in winter is normal; across the river from Hyesan is China's Changbai.
